input.text: [lane-vole] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: if a service moves to a new server, users keep being sent to the old one, causing outages or errors. (2) Slow recovery and failover: when you change records to route around a fault, the change takes longer to reach users. (3) Longer exposure to bad data: a poisoned or hijacked answer stays in the cache for longer before it expires, so more people are affected.

Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (Universally Unique Identifier, version 7) as a primary key:

(1) It is ordered by time, so new rows land near the end of the index and inserts stay fast. The cost is that the key reveals when the row was created.

(2) It takes 16 bytes, which is more than a typical integer key. Indexes and foreign keys therefore use more space and memory.

(1) It passes and fails on the same code. A plain re-run with no change gives a different result.
(2) The failure depends on things outside the code, such as timing, test order, shared data or the machine used. It often goes away when the test is run alone.

A test that really fails does so every time, for the same reason.

input.text: [lane-vole] A lease-based lock gives a worker the lock for a set time, after which it expires. Clock skew means two machines disagree about what time it is. If the lock holder's clock runs slow, it believes its lease is still valid after the server has already expired it and given the lock to someone else. Then two workers act at once, which the lock was meant to prevent. A common fix is a fencing token, a rising number that the protected resource checks, so stale holders are rejected.

Clock skew breaks lease-based locks because the lock depends on every machine agreeing about the time.

A lease gives a worker the lock for a set time, after which it expires. Clock skew means two machines disagree about what time it is. Suppose the lock holder's clock runs slow. It believes its lease is still valid after the server has already expired it and given the lock to someone else. Two workers then act at once, which is what the lock was meant to prevent.

A common fix is a fencing token. This is a number that rises with each new lock holder. The protected resource checks it and rejects stale holders.

I've recorded this in Studio as step 10 with `brief_seen="verbatim"`.
